Title: Festival of Flame
Summary:
The sun hung low over Eldenhold’s amber skyline, its rays gilding the cobbled streets as music drifted lazily from colorful stalls and taverns. The Festival of Flame had returned again—twenty years since the fall of Asmodeus, and the city thrummed with celebration. Streamers danced on warm gusts, children sprinted between merchant booths, and ale flowed freely in honor of Lady Arabelle Thorne, the paladin whose sword helped end an infernal age.
A long table stood in the heart of the market square, reserved for Arabelle’s “special guests.” One by one, the misfit heroes arrived.
Grenak Goateater—hulking orc, lover of ale, and breaker of doors—grunted as he elbowed his friend. “Reese, we should find a pub.”
Reese, ever the weary warlock with haunted eyes, smirked. “Always thirsty, Grenak. But maybe we find the demons first, drinks second.”
They were joined by others: Valen Silverpalm, charming and righteous; Bruno Mars, the velvet-voiced rogue with too many lovers and even more enemies; Mruno, sly and paranoid, trailing whispers of debt and intrigue; and Kelsynk Tchotchke, the lover of chaos and gadgets.
Mugs were raised. Grenak persuaded a vendor for extra mead with a glare and a grin, while the group collectively endured the ramblings of Old Man Griggs, a mad prophet rooting through trash for visions and rat bones.
“The rings,” Griggs muttered, his eyes unfocused. “The rings are breaking. The stars are hungry.”
Reese offered him food. Valen offered him compassion. Grinak offered him suspicion.
And then, like a storm in boots, she arrived.
Lady Arabelle Thorne.
Clad in ceremonial armor, her presence turned heads and hushed mouths. “My favorite little stormfront,” she greeted them. “Try not to level a district before I’ve finished my speech.”
There were nods, a few sheepish grins, and a dozen denials of culpability.
The square bustled with chaos: a goblin bard tuned a lute, a drow watched from the shadows, and a halfling raged against a vendor whose ale turned drinkers... green.
Grinak, green himself, was unimpressed. “Green is good color. Strong color.”
Reese, with a dry tone, added, “Unless it’s your liver.”
Meanwhile, Bruno flirted poorly with Lena the barmaid, earning a pat on the shoulder and a pitying, “You’re such a good friend.”
Elsewhere, Grenak found a worthy challenge—a half-orc soldier who drank like a dragon and arm-wrestled like a god. She bested him once, but not twice, and with each round they shared another tankard and another laugh.
Then the celebration darkened.
Lady Arabelle took the stage, voice booming over the crowd. “Twenty years ago, we shattered the infernal chain. Today, we celebrate unity—”
A boy, no older than eight, strolled into view, tossing an egg. Not just any egg—flames flickered beneath the shell. All eyes turned as he approached a jewelry vendor.
Mruno was the first to move, crafting a spectral image of a guard to deter the boy. It failed.
Grenak, ever the blunt instrument, roared, “No waste food!” The boy froze, terrified.
Valen knelt to reason with him. “Son, what are you doing?”
The boy’s voice cracked. “That vendor... he ruined my family. He threw us out. Someone said this egg would teach the nobles a lesson.”
The party exchanged glances. Someone was playing a deeper game.
Valen stepped forward, trying to stop the throw, and slapped the egg out of the boy’s hand, much to the distain of the crowd. Dockworkers surged forward, angry and misinformed, assuming the heroes were bullying a child. Fists clenched. Weapons loosened.
“Grenak wanted fight,” he muttered, flexing.
“Well,” Reese sighed, “happy festival.”
The brawl began.

Title: Fear, Flight, and the Girl Named Susie
Summary: Our heroes begin in classic Grenak fashion: fists first, questions never. A brawl erupts with a group of dockworkers—just what Grenak was hoping for. Reese wastes no time, casting Fear on the gang. Five dockworkers immediately lose their nerve and flee, trembling. Amid the chaos, Valen swings and misses, then recovers with a crack of his staff. Mruno adds insult to injury—literally—by hurling pointed mockery at the last standing dockworker.As the terrified crew scatters, Valen catches one with a parting shot to the back. Grenak casually walks up to another and delivers a devastating... slap, reducing the poor soul to tears. The dockworkers scatter like leaves in a storm.After the dust settles, Mruno convinces Grenak to mark his victory by peeing in the town’s decorative fountain. Grenak obliges—stealthily, of course—and then, with a perfectly timed backhand, knocks Pip Thistlesown (the town’s resident annoyance) straight into the very spot he’d just christened.Unfortunately, Lady Arabella is mid-speech when chaos ignites once more. The crowd turns into a mob. Mruno and Valen try to talk them down—moderately successful, but only half the crowd listens. Things spiral.Enter General Thornvale, who storms the scene and declares martial law. With a pointed finger, he summons the party. Not interested in a formal chat with military brass, the group slips away like shadows and vanishes into the night.Their new goal? Demon hunting.Valen mentions a demon-infested island to the west, and the party agrees to head for Port Town to secure passage. Along the road, Mruno and Grenak engage in a heated singing competition. Grenak, with the overconfidence of someone who peaked in elementary school talent shows, is thoroughly outperformed by Mruno’s bardic flair.The road leads them through the ghost town of Ashenvale, now abandoned save for a lone tavern and an eerily calm eight-year-old girl named Susie. She warns them the town is cursed—zombies and ghosts roam freely here.And that’s where we leave our party: on the edge of something undead, cursed, and probably extremely inconvenient.

Title: Little Susie and Mruno’s Soiled Pants
Summary: The tavern was too clean.That was the first thing the party noticed as they stepped inside the oddly pristine inn of a seemingly deserted village. Dust should have been thick. Cobwebs should have clung to every rafter. Instead, the place sparkled, polished to a shine by the hands of a single occupant: an eight-year-old girl named Susie.She greeted them with eerie cheerfulness. Grenak Goateater, ever the heart-on-his-sleeve barbarian, decided she needed a mentor—and who better than him? He offered to teach her the sacred arts of drinking and fighting. Reese, as always, stood silently, his cold gaze distant. His mind was elsewhere—on the island, on the demons, on vengeance. Mruno Bars, though, couldn’t shake his suspicions. Something about the girl felt off. Off enough that he lifted his hand and dispelled her magical veil.The truth unfolded before them like a nightmare.Susie shrieked and transformed, her small form morphing into something demonic. Red skin stretched over rippling muscle, horns curled from her brow, and her once-innocent dress clung in tattered remnants. Her head remained disarmingly small. Reese cursed her. Mruno ran for cover. Valen struck with a flurry of monk-trained fists—and missed every one.Grenak’s betrayal hit him hard. This was his protégé. His apprentice of booze and battle. And now? Now he got to kill a demon. Giddy with bloodlust, he roared into rage, mocked her tiny horns, and cleaved her with his greataxe—twice.Mruno hurled insult after insult, dancing at a distance.In fury, the demon Susie turned her magic on them. She frightened Grenak, attempted to rip Reese’s soul from his chest, and was only barely deflected by his blade. Reese retaliated, striking true, then missing his second swing with smug overconfidence. Valen landed blows in a fury, one connecting clean with her nose.Grenak, even while terrified, swallowed ng his greataxe in his rage. Mruno, ever the performer, inspired Reese, mocked Susie again, then dramatically sat to “watch the show.”Big mistake.Susie vanished into shadow, reappearing behind Mruno. She unleashed a wave of terror, blinding and frightening everyone but Valen. Mruno screamed and cast Hellish Rebuke. Flames licked across her skin, and she absorbed the fire with a hiss. Reese stood frozen. Valen shot radiant energy and struck her, leaving her visibly wounded.Grenak, still shaking, hurled handaxes—which whizzed dangerously close to Mruno’s head. Mruno bolted, going invisible, sliding between Grenak’s legs, and fleeing to the safety of the party.Susie teleported to Valen and struck him down nearly dead. Mruno, received the brunt of her psychic scream—and collapsed. Reese, still blind and terrified, phased through her like a ghost, striking from behind with his rapier. Susie spun on him, claws lashing out, and only missed his heart by inches.Valen, now bloodied and desperate, pulled his daggers. Miss. Miss. He hurled them down in frustration—and swung his fists that finally struck true, hitting her head. She staggered and fell, her head slamming against the bar.It was over.The town stirred.As the demon died, the air shifted. Voices and movement returned to the streets. Reese stabilized Mruno’s broken body. Mruno awoke to Grenak teasing him for wetting himself in fear. Unshaken, Mruno adjusted his cloak with a flourish, changed his pants, and restored his pride with practiced flair.Before they stepped outside, Mruno cast Protection from Evil on Grenak. Valen peeked through the window and saw villagers wandering aimlessly. One man recalled eating dinner… and then falling asleep… and being pulled from his body.They learned Susie had been adopted by the tavern owners. The couple had suspected something odd about her but never guessed she was a demon. In thanks for freeing them, they offered the party free food and lodging.Over dinner, Mruno asked to perform as part of their payment. The villagers, recognizing him, mentioned rumors—about the Silken Sonics having a new lead singer: Dark Bronson. Mruno scoffed. Denied it. Deflected. But they pressed on. The band was touring the coast. Word was: they were near Port Town.Mruno took the news with a flick of his cloak and an uneasy glint in his eye.Later, while the others turned in for the night, Mruno attempted to find romance among the inn’s guests. He struck out. Badly.And the village, finally freed from the demon’s grip, slept under the quiet eye of the moon.

Title: Of Banjos, Bards, and Billy Bumblers
Summary:
The tavern, freshly freed from demonic possession, was eerily peaceful at dawn. The air was thick with the smell of eggs, wood polish, and uneasy calm. Downstairs, Grenak Goateater thudded into the common room, hungry and half-alert.
He wasn’t alone.
Seated quietly on a bench near the wall was a stranger: wide-brimmed hat, long duster coat, a worn horn case at his side. His name was Roland Blackstone—a ranger with a purpose, and a presence like still water before a storm.
Grenak, in his usual tactless glory, plopped down next to Roland, causing the bench to seesaw dangerously. Roland didn’t flinch.
“Pass the salt and pepper?” Grenak grunted.
Roland obliged.
“Thanks,” Grenak added. “Reese’s wife is dead, you know.”
Right on cue, Reese descended the stairs like a brooding wraith. The mention of his wife cut deeper than the salt. He said nothing, just glared at the table and sat heavily—dark eyes, darker thoughts.
Then came Valen, who wisely sat across the table to preserve the structural integrity of the bench. He offered Roland a polite smile and asked how the eggs were.
Mruno Bars entered last, cloak trailing behind him, still adjusting the feather in his cap. He took a seat beside Reese—leaving a deliberate gap. Just enough room for Reese’s late wife. Another jab. Another motherless joke. Another scowl from Reese.
Talk turned to Roland, who introduced himself properly. He was hunting a demon called Towerheart, and he’d traveled far for the scent. When asked about music, he casually dropped, “Oh, I’ve heard the Silken Sonics are incredible now. Ever since Dark Bronson joined.”
The tension snapped.
Mruno’s fingers curled around his spoon. The mention of that name was a slap to the ego. His band, his legacy—now fronted by a diva wrapped in glitter and blasphemy? No. Unacceptable.
Their waitress, Marina, arrived then—young, energetic, hopelessly enamored with Mruno. She gushed, she swooned, she giggled. Mruno brushed her off, promising he might perform for her later. Maybe.
Then her sister stormed in.
Carly.
Sharp as broken glass and just as subtle. She tore into Mruno with biting sarcasm.
“You? Perform? You squawk, not sing.”
The whole table winced.
Mruno, flustered and challenged, made a bet. If he could pack the tavern and put on a show that impressed her, she’d have to go on a date with him.
Carlysmirked. “Fine. Impress me.”
Thus, a band was born.
Grenak tried drums—first with fists. It sounded like furniture falling downstairs. Mruno offered him spoons instead. The rhythm clicked. Grenak grinned.
Roland had an old horn—his personal one—but refused to play it. It meant too much. Fortunately, the bartender had a backup horn stashed under the bar. They handed it to Roland… and it squeaked. Inside was a mouse, snug and fluffy. Once evicted, the horn played true. Roland found his sound.
Valen grabbed a jug, declared it his instrument, and the more he drank, the better it sounded. It worked disturbingly well.
Reese, silent as ever, brought out a fiddle. He played with eerie grace. Cold, haunting, perfect.
As they practiced, Carly, impressed despite herself, agreed to join on banjo.
One problem remained: the Silken Sonics were coming to town that night—and Dark Bronson would recognize Mruno instantly. A plan was needed.
Mruno put together a disguise so convincing, even Grenak did a double take. The group had to explain that just because it doesn’t look like Mruno doesn’t mean it isn’t. It wasn’t until the disguised Mruno made a perfectly-timed, brutal joke about Reese’s wife that Grenak finally nodded.
“That’s him,” he said. “Only Mruno would say something that mean.”
With the band assembled, it was time to spread the word. Posters were needed.
Valen and Mruno’s were practically professional—bold fonts, catchy phrasing, artistic flair. Grenak’s were passable, mostly because people were too scared to criticize them. Reese’s were minimalist and dark, like his soul.
Roland’s?
They looked like his Billy-Bumbler made them. With its feet. While chewing crayons.
But it didn’t matter. The posters were up. The tavern was buzzing. The Silken Sonics were coming. The band had no name, but they had heart, and a show to steal.
Tonight, they wouldn’t face demons.
Tonight, they’d face the crowd.

Title: Battle of Bards
Summary:
The afternoon haze settled over Ashenvale as the party returned to the tavern, still glowing from a day of shameless self-promotion. They’d scattered across the town, hyping the long-awaited debut of their band, Punch Drunk Love. Spirits were high, jokes were flowing, and Mruno Bars felt ready for anything.
Until the bartender dropped the news.
The Silken Sonics had arrived early. What was meant to be tomorrow’s headline act had pushed up to tonight. The bar owner shrugged, counting a fat purse. “They paid extra,” he said. “Wanted the room now. But hey—still need an opener.”
Mruno narrowed his eyes. “No opener. Let’s make it a bard-off.”
The deal was struck.
By sundown, the tavern was packed—elbow-to-elbow with fans, travelers, curious locals, and some rowdy nobility slumming it for a night of wild entertainment. As the crowd roared louder, Mruno found Marina at the bar.
“Well,” she said, leaning close with a half-smile, “looks like you packed the place. Guess that means you win the date.”
Mruno glanced at the crowd—not with hesitation, but with principle. He knew he could’ve filled this place on his own. But with the Silken Sonics suddenly in the mix, the numbers were skewed, and he wasn’t going to claim a victory that wasn’t entirely his.
“Nah,” he said gently. “Not like this. Doesn’t feel right. Maybe next time.”
Marina tilted her head, surprised. “You’d come back? Just to see me?”
He didn’t answer. Didn’t have to.
Then the doors flew open.
Six Golden Mentor Guild agents stepped inside, dressed like secret blades—slick black leather, slicker hair, eyes scanning the room like wolves in velvet. Behind them, with the force of a parade and the grace of a glitter bomb, came Dark Bronson.
He was a nightmare in red and pink—heart-shaped glasses, maroon fur-lined jacket hanging open over a chest that really didn’t need to be seen, cape trailing like a peacock’s tail on fire. Every step screamed, I am the moment. The Silken Sonics followed behind him like chained interns, clad in stiff corporate uniforms and the look of people who had long since given up on joy.
Bronson took the stage and belted out a diss track aimed at Mruno Bars—an off-key, self-indulgent mess of ego and glitter. The lyrics made no sense. The rhythm was worse. But Bronson performed like he thought he was saving the world. A few polite claps echoed in the stunned silence.
Then Punch Drunk Love took the stage.
Mruno. Reese. Grenak. Valen. Roland. And Marina on banjo. They launched into their rowdy, infectious anthem: “Fight and Fight and Drink.” And the tavern exploded.
Carly and her friends danced on benches, screaming like fans at a god’s coronation. One of them—a fedora-wearing, flamboyant blur of limbs—cheered so hard he nearly passed out. Bronson watched from the side, seething.
As the song ended, Bronson spat insults from across the floor. But nobody cared.
Then came the agents.
Guild security moved in, slow and deliberate. Their eyes locked on Mruno. No room for doubt now—this was a trap.
Someone in the party whispered a spell. Darkness burst through the tavern, and chaos followed. Screams. Stumbling. A table flipped. Drinks splashed. Someone punched a man entirely by accident. It was glorious.
In the confusion, Carly appeared at Mruno’s side. “I know a secret way out—but I want a kiss!”
Mruno paused—his hand still holding Marina’s. “Fine,” he grunted. “Later.”
She grinned like she’d won the lottery and led them through the riot.
Outside, in the quiet of a back alley, she stopped him. “Promise is a promise.”
Before he could dodge, she grabbed his collar and kissed him—hard, dramatic, and far too long. When it ended, she just sighed. “Wow…”
Marina was watching. And her smile was gone.
“You kissed her?” she asked flatly. Mruno opened his mouth to speak, but she cut him off.
“It’s fine,” she said. “Really. I’ve been figuring stuff out. And I think… I don’t think I like guys. I think I’m good. But hey—thanks for helping me realize it.”
Then she turned and walked back toward the chaos.
Behind them, the tavern continued to collapse. Chairs were flying. Fans were screaming. And somewhere inside, Dark Bronson was likely trying to start a second set.
Punch Drunk Love slipped away into the night.
Two towns. Two riots. Zero regrets.
Next stop: Port Town—the edge of civilization and the gateway to a cursed island crawling with demons. The sea was calling, and the show was far from over.

Title: The Spy in the Road
Summary:
Last time on Sunspire

The aftermath of Ashenvale still smoking behind them, our trouble-magnets set out for Port Town—about a day and a half on foot if nothing else explodes. That “if” doesn’t last long.

On the way out of Ashenvale, the group decides morale (and stomachs) come first. Reese follows his nose to a back-alley stand with the “best fried squirrel in town,” plus enough ale to rinse out the guilt. They try to sneak it, fail as a group, and suddenly there’s an audience—angry locals, and Dark Bronson’s reputation hanging in the air like last night’s bad song. Mruno works the crowd, Grenak looms, and the heat eases just enough for them to grab food, top off on courage, and keep moving.

Word travels faster than they do. The Golden Minotaur Guild is sniffing around for Mruno, so he keeps his disguise on: cloak up, fake beard, fake nose—the whole “not Mruno Bars” package. Unfortunately, the kit sheds like a moulting ferret. The nose keeps falling off. After a few disastrous re-applications, Grenak solves it in the most Grenak way possible: lick, stick, done. It’s gross. It works. They march.

They choose the main road for speed. Roland proposes camping in the road “to invite a good fight,” Valen vetoes, and they compromise: Grenak sleeps in the road anyway, everyone else takes the bushes. Roland sets an Alarm around the big orc and calls it a night.

The spell pays off. Sometime past midnight the Alarm thrums and the party goes still. Hoofbeats. Six riders in black leather pass by, not Minotaur Guild—Black Talon mercenaries. Assassins for hire. They never spot the group and keep heading the same direction as our heroes: Port Town. It’s a quiet win, but it isn’t comforting.

Dawn brings a different kind of problem. Roland—ex-military—finally shares the rumor that’s been chewing on him: a trusted contact told him someone in the party is a spy. No proof, no name, just a warning. Cue chaos. Insight checks and side-eyes fly. Valen misreads everything, Mruno tries to read everyone, Grenak tries intimidation-by-vocabulary, and Reese pushes to keep people moving. In the end, nobody’s cleared, nobody’s condemned, and they walk on with the question still hitchhiking in the back of everyone’s mind.

By afternoon the road spills them out onto the coast. Port Town is a wind-chewed sprawl of leaning piers, gulls that scream like old hinges, and the kind of faces that don’t look up unless steel or coin makes them. The group clocks a few landmarks: a bent sign for a rough tavern and boarding house called The Bent Coin, a smithy that sounds like a rumor mill, and, more importantly, Minotaur Guild types working the docks. Cloaks go up, disguises go tighter—especially around Mruno’s face hardware—and they angle for the tavern.

Inside the Bent Coin, the air is thick with low voices and flat ale. A bored guard plays at being background noise. The room notes the strangers, then carefully remembers other things to do. One table stands out: a bronze Dragonborn sits with a half-orc, deep in conversation. Dragonborn are rare here; rare things draw attention—even if you try not to stare.

The party takes stock. They’re hungry, tired, being hunted by at least two different outfits, and now sharing a room with two very interesting strangers. The Minotaur Guild is on the docks, the Black Talons are on the road behind them, and somewhere out there a nameless “trusted contact” swears a spy walks among them.

That’s where we leave them: boots under a battered table at the Bent Coin, trying to look small while the world around them gets bigger teeth. Next stop—if they can sit still long enough to plan it—finding a ship and a way forward that doesn’t end with rope, riot, or both.
